Association Finance & Reserves

mainEntity.name: How much should our association keep in reserves?

acceptedAnswer.text: Illinois requires condominium associations to fund reserves reasonable for the repair and replacement of common elements, judged against the age and condition of the building’s components, unless owners have voted to waive it. The statute sets no number, which is why a reserve study matters: it inventories components with remaining useful lives and replacement costs, then converts them into a funding plan a board can defend to owners.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between a special assessment and a reserve?

acceptedAnswer.text: A reserve is money collected steadily in advance for work everyone knows is coming. A special assessment is money collected suddenly for work that arrived before the reserve did. They fund the same repairs — the difference is whether owners had years to absorb the cost or weeks. Most special assessments are a reserve-funding decision made years earlier, catching up.

mainEntity.name: When should the board involve the attorney on collections?

acceptedAnswer.text: Adopt a written collection policy in advance with defined trigger points, then follow it identically for every owner. Statements and late notices are administrative. Once the matter reaches a formal demand, a lien, or any action affecting possession, it carries statutory notice requirements and belongs with association counsel. What the board controls is the policy and the trigger; what counsel controls is the legal step.

mainEntity.name: Why does our insurance keep costing more?

acceptedAnswer.text: Illinois associations have faced sustained premium increases driven by claims history, replacement-cost inflation on building materials, deductible structures, and reinsurance markets that price weather risk. Boards have less control over the market than over their own exposure: current appraisals, documented maintenance, resolved deferred repairs, and a clean claims record all affect what an underwriter offers at renewal.

Illinois Condo Insurance Deductibles: When Can the Board Charge an Owner?

Master policy deductibles have climbed, and a single water loss can leave a five-figure bill. Illinois law gives condo boards three options for who pays it. Here is how each one works and the step boards most often skip.
Keeping Reserves Safe: FDIC Limits for Illinois Associations

A reserve fund that has grown past $250,000 at a single bank is partly uninsured, no matter how many owners the association has. Here is how FDIC coverage works for associations and what a reserve investment policy should cover.
Fidelity Insurance for Illinois Associations and Their Manager

Fidelity coverage is the policy that pays when someone steals association money. Illinois sets requirements for both the association and its management company, and one of those rules changed in July 2026.
Can Illinois Condo Owners Demand an Independent Audit?

A group of owners asks the board for an independent audit and says the law requires it. Before the board answers, it helps to know exactly what the Condominium Property Act does and does not say about audits.
Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac Raise the Condo Reserve Minimum to 15%: What Boards Must Do for the 2027 Budget

For loan applications dated on or after January 4, 2027, Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac will look for a replacement-reserve allocation of at least 15% of budgeted assessment income — up from 10%. The 2027 budget your board adopts this fall decides whether buyers in your building can get a conventional loan.

Reasonable Reserves Under Illinois Condo Law
